newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: ALPINE SKIING-HARD WEEK BEGINS FOR WORLD CUP DOWNHILLERS.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-HARD WEEK BEGINS FOR WORLD CUP DOWNHILLERS.

text.p: Luc Alphand and Kristian Ghedina know that their respective hopes of winning the World Cup downhill title depend on which of them can better endure the hardships of the coming week.
The Wengen downhill on Saturday, on the famed Lauberhorn, kicks off a tough week for the Alpine ski racers.
From Wengen they will move directly to Kitzbuehel for a double downhill on the treacherous Streif.
If Kitzbuehel is a test of courage then Wengen, the longest downhill on the circuit at 4.2 kms, is a test of strength and endurance.
But the Lauberhorn can be tricky too and the death of Austria's Gernot Reinstadler in a training run crash in 1991 is ever-present on skiers' minds.

While caution is an unfamilar concept to most downhillers, Alphand and Ghedina, the two principal figures in the battle for the downhill crown, are both planning to show a little restraint with the world championships only two weeks away.

"I'm playing it safe until Sestriere and then I'll go for it," said Frenchman Alphand, the reigning World Cup downhill champion. "Winning a gold medal in Sestriere is my goal this season. I'll go for wins after the championships.
"The way Kristian is skiing that's what I will have to do to keep the title. He's my pal when he's behind me but once he's in front things change."
Alphand's cautious tone may stem partially from his brush with disaster last weekend in Chamonix.
Although he was able to recover from a bad mistake and continue unscathed to finish a respectable fifth behind winner Ghedina, the Frenchman said later that he saw his career pass before his eyes.
"Unfortunately I lost many points in Chamonix because of my mistake," said Alphand. "But my mistake could have turned into a nasty injury so I can't complain."
Alphand and Ghedina have split the last four races with two wins apiece and share the lead in the downhill standings with 365 points.
"I hope my great shape holds until Sestriere because that's my main goal," said Ghedina, who became the most successful World Cup downhiller in Italian history with his sixth career win in Chamonix.
Any hesitation by Ghedina or Alphand will open the door for Austria's frustrated downhillers.

From the start of the season the Austrians have looked to dominate Alpine skiing's glamour event but, with the exception of a sweep of the podium in Val d'Isere, they have been unable to translate their success in training to races.
The beleaguered Swiss will also be looking to turn their season around.

William Besse's second place in Bormio was the only appearance by a Swiss on the downhill podium this season and the first since Bruno Kernen produced back-to-back wins on home snow at Veysonnaz last year.
The last time races were staged at this Swiss resort in 1995 it was an all-Italian weekend with Ghedina and slalom king Alberto Tomba both registering wins.

While Ghedina remains in the hunt for a second consecutive victory, Tomba, still recovering from influenza that forced him out of the second leg of last weekend's giant slalom in Chamonix, has yet to indicate whether he will even race in Sunday's slalom.
Tomba, who crashed heavily in pre-season training and injured a wrist and knee, has struggled to get back to his old form and has completed only two slaloms this season.

The Italian, who captured the giant and slalom world titles in Spain last year, was second in a slalom on his season's debut at Madonna di Campiglio before Christmas but failed to finish a giant slalom in Kranjska Gora, Slovenia, on January 5.
Adding insult to injury, he tumbled out of the World Cup giant slalom top 15 rankings for the first time in 10 years on Tuesday, after skipping a race in Adelboden.

Whether Tomba makes an appearance or not, the spotlight will fall on Austria's Thomas Sykora who has dominated the slalom this season as the flamboyant Italian once did, winning four out of five events.
Switzerland's Michael von Gruenigen will have to egual or better his fourth place finish in Chamonix if he hopes to cling to his lead in the overall standings.
Von Gruenigen, who has been on the podium in five of the six giant slaloms this season, holds a slim, 26-point advantage over Norwegian all-rounder Kjetil Andre Aamodt.
